summary: Specifies a password-based HTTP authentication scheme that provides true mutual authentication between client and server, unlike Basic and Digest. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: Both you and the website prove you know the secret, so you also know the site is real.

subtitle: Password authentication where client and server both prove they know the secret.

tldr.problem: Basic and Digest HTTP authentication are vulnerable to offline password attacks and phishing. Users cannot verify that they are authenticating to the real server.
tldr.mechanism: The Mutual scheme uses password-based authenticated key exchange (PAKE) to create a shared session secret. Both client and server must prove they know the password; neither reveals the password itself.
tldr.outcome: Neither party can impersonate the other without knowing the password. The session secret protects subsequent requests from tampering. Phishing attacks fail because the fake server cannot complete the authentication.

today: RFC 8120 specifies an Experimental authentication protocol for HTTP. While it provides strong mutual authentication, adoption has been limited. Most web systems continue using TLS with Basic or session-based authentication. The protocol remains a reference for how to achieve true mutual authentication with passwords.

sections.title: Introduction and Security Problems
sections.content:
Password-based authentication for HTTP faces several security challenges. Basic authentication sends passwords in plain text (unless wrapped in TLS). Digest authentication hides the password with a hash, but if the password is weak or common, an attacker can compute hash values offline and compare them to captured traffic.

Transport Layer Security (TLS) protects passwords on the wire, but does not protect against phishing. If a user is tricked into visiting a malicious website, they will send their real password to the attacker's server. Once captured, an attacker can use the password to impersonate the user on the legitimate site.

The Mutual authentication scheme solves these problems by implementing password-based authenticated key exchange. No password information is transmitted. Both the client and server must prove they possess the correct password-derived secret. A phishing attacker cannot trick a user into thinking a fake site is real, because the fake site will fail the mutual authentication check.
sections.plainLanguage: Basic authentication is like leaving your key visible. Digest hides it with math, but attackers can still guess it offline. Mutual authentication is different: you and the website both do a secret handshake that proves you both know the key, and neither side ever sends the key itself.

sections.title: Protocol Flow and Message Exchange
sections.content:
The Mutual authentication protocol uses six types of messages. First, a client requests a protected resource. The server responds with a 401-INIT message requesting authentication and specifying the algorithm and validation method.

Second, the client sends a req-KEX-C1 message initiating a key exchange with its username and client key value (K_c1). The server responds with a 401-KEX-S1 message containing the server key value (K_s1) and a session identifier (sid).

At this point, both peers independently compute a shared session secret (z) using the exchanged values. Only when both peers used secrets derived from the same password will their session secrets match.

Third, the client sends a req-VFY-C message with a verification value (VK_c) computed from the session secret. The server verifies this value. If correct, the server responds with a 200-VFY-S message containing its own verification value (VK_s). The client verifies VK_s to confirm the server knows the correct password.

In typical cases, this exchange requires three HTTP request-response pairs. Optimizations reduce this to two pairs if the client anticipates authentication, or one pair if reusing an existing session.
sections.plainLanguage: The handshake has three parts. First, client says 'let's prove we both know the password'. Second, they exchange secret numbers. Third, they each prove they computed the same secret correctly. If both proofs work, they trust each other.

sections.title: Message Format and Headers
sections.content:
Mutual authentication uses three HTTP headers. The server sends challenges in WWW-Authenticate headers with Mutual authentication challenges. Clients send credentials in Authorization headers with Mutual authentication parameters. Successful responses carry Authentication-Info headers.

All parameters are name-value pairs following HTTP syntax. Parameters include version (always '1'), algorithm (specifying the cryptographic algorithm), validation (the method to verify server identity), realm (the authentication scope), and user (the client's username).

Key exchange and verification values are encoded as either base64-fixed-number or hex-fixed-number depending on the algorithm. Session identifiers (sid) are random hex numbers with at least 80 bits of uniqueness. Nonce numbers (nc) track request ordering to prevent replay attacks and help servers detect stale sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages have a standard format with named fields. Some fields carry the secret handshake numbers, some identify which math algorithm is being used, and some prevent cheating by tracking request order.

sections.title: Realms, Sessions, and Host Validation
sections.content:
An authentication realm is a set of resources (URIs) for which the same username and password are valid. Each realm is identified by three components: an algorithm, an authentication scope, and a realm name.

Authentication scopes can be single-server type (scheme://host:port), single-host type (host only), or wildcard-domain type (*.domain). This allows credentials to be shared across protocols and ports but remain isolated per host or domain.

Sessions are established during key exchange and are local to each server and realm. A session's secret (z) is reused for multiple requests within the same session's lifetime. Clients maintain session identifiers and use nonce numbers to prevent replay attacks and enable duplicate detection.

Host validation binds authentication to the underlying transport. The 'host' validation method uses the server's scheme, host, and port. The 'tls-server-end-point' method uses the TLS certificate's hash. The 'tls-unique' method uses TLS Finished message values. This prevents man-in-the-middle attacks and ensures the authentication is tied to the intended server.
sections.plainLanguage: A realm is a login area. Sessions remember you so you do not have to log in for every click. Host validation makes sure you are talking to the real server, not an imposter.

sections.title: Security Properties and Client Decision Logic
sections.content:
The protocol provides strong mutual authentication. The password is never transmitted or derivable from the transmitted values. A server cannot impersonate a legitimate user without knowing the correct password. A client cannot be deceived by a fake server claiming to be legitimate.

To securely implement the protocol, clients must follow strict rules. A 200-VFY-S response is only accepted as a response to a req-VFY-C request. The server's verification value (VK_s) must be checked before accepting the response. If an attacker modifies the response or the verification fails, the client must reject the entire response including its content.

Clients must also reject 'normal responses' (responses without authentication headers) if they were expecting authentication. They must track session state and reject responses that do not match the expected authentication realm. A state machine with strict transitions prevents clients from accepting out-of-order messages or accepting responses in unexpected situations.
sections.plainLanguage: The security comes from the math: only someone with the right password can compute the right answers. Clients must be strict about what responses they accept and must always verify the server's proof.

sections.title: Extensions and Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
The protocol defines a framework that can be extended with new algorithms. RFC 8121 specifies cryptographic algorithms based on Key Agreement Mechanism 3 (KAM3), using discrete-logarithm and elliptic-curve groups with SHA-256 and SHA-512 hash functions.

Channel binding ties authentication to the underlying transport layer, preventing attacker relays. Application-level channel binding allows applications to derive shared secrets from the Mutual authentication session to protect higher-layer operations.

The protocol supports proxy authentication by replacing status codes and headers appropriately (using 407 Proxy Authentication Required and Proxy-Authenticate headers). The 'auth-scope' is fixed to the proxy's hostname in this case.

String preparation using PRECIS profiles ensures usernames and passwords are normalized for interoperability. Servers should prepare credentials the same way during user registration.
sections.plainLanguage: The basic scheme can be extended with different math. You can also bind the authentication to TLS to be extra safe, or use it with proxies. Usernames and passwords should be formatted consistently.
